Meanwhile, every database query carries hidden cost: disk seeks, lock waits, and repeated planning. A cache intercepts that cost by storing results near the reader, so cached rows answer later requests without touching storage; this idea shapes modern system design.

However, correctness now becomes the hard part. Stale entries mislead readers, so teams pick a strategy: expire keys after a short window, or invalidate them the moment a write lands. Write-through designs update store and cache together, while write-behind buffers changes; both trade risk against speed. Measuring cache hit ratio guides every later tuning decision.

Along with gains, though, a shortcut brings tricky bugs. RAM stays small, so old data sits around too long, and a warm copy may drift far from what SQL truly holds. Split loading across many hosts, watch for churn, and log all faults.

Finally, treat the cache as a load reducer, never as truth; measure, expire wisely, and your tuning work is done.
